name: Gorilla Time-Series Compression: Delta-of-Delta & XOR Floats
tagline: Compressing 16-byte (timestamp, float64) telemetry points down to ~1.37 bytes in streaming O(1) memory.
purpose: Understand why general-purpose compression like Zstd/LZ4 fails on streaming 2-hour time-series blocks, and how Facebook Gorilla's Delta-of-Delta timestamps + IEEE-754 XOR float encoding achieve ~11x lossless compression.

prerequisites.title: IEEE-754 64-Bit Floating Point Layout
prerequisites.summary: Know that a `float64` packs 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, and 52 mantissa bits—and nearby values share almost identical upper bits.

prerequisites.title: Bit-Level Streaming Buffers
prerequisites.summary: Understand writing variable-width bitfields (1 bit, 7 bits, 9 bits) rather than byte-aligned integers.

spark.summary: Gorilla encodes regular-interval timestamps in 1 bit via Delta-of-Delta and compresses slowly changing IEEE-754 floats via XOR bit-windows, shrinking 16-byte samples to ~1.37 bytes.
spark.keyTakeaway: When storing high-frequency monitoring telemetry in RAM for fast dashboard queries, use Gorilla's Delta-of-Delta + XOR streaming compression per series chunk so you get ~11x memory savings without batching delays.
spark.byteSummary:
An uncompressed `(int64 timestamp, float64 value)` data point takes 16 bytes. At 10M points/sec, keeping just 2 hours of hot telemetry in RAM for fast alerting would require 1.15 TB of DRAM. Running Zstd over tiny per-series arrays either adds CPU latency or requires buffering large batches that delay real-time reads.

Facebook's Gorilla paper introduced two streaming bit-level tricks that compress each point on arrival in O(1) time. First, for timestamps, metrics arrive at regular intervals (e.g., every 60s). Instead of storing `t_n`, Gorilla computes the Delta-of-Delta `D = (t_n - t_{n-1}) - (t_{n-1} - t_{n-2})`. When `D == 0` (~96% of points), it writes a single `'0'` bit; small jitter fits in 7-, 9-, or 12-bit buckets.

Second, for values, consecutive `float64` readings (like CPU = 42.1% -> 42.3%) share the same sign, exponent, and upper mantissa bits. Gorilla computes `xor = v_{n-1} ^ v_n`. If `xor == 0`, it emits a single `'0'` bit. Otherwise, it reuses the previous XOR's leading/trailing zero window (2 control bits + meaningful bits) or writes a 5-bit leading-zero count + 6-bit length + meaningful bits—averaging ~1.37 bytes per `(timestamp, value)` pair.

learningJourney.title: P · Problem & Why Uncompressed Telemetry Blows Up RAM
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Quantifies the 16-byte/point memory wall and why batch codecs hurt real-time alerting.

explanation.foundation: Every raw metric sample is 8 bytes for the Unix timestamp + 8 bytes for the `float64` value = 16 bytes.
explanation.core: At 10M samples/sec, 2 hours (7,200 seconds) of hot operational metrics equals 72 billion points = 1.152 TB of raw DRAM before any index overhead. Compressing with gzip/Zstd across 10M separate series buffers either forces tiny 100-byte blocks (poor ratio) or delays flushing until buffers fill.
explanation.deepDive: Gorilla compresses bit-by-bit as each sample arrives into an append-only 2-hour chunk per series, allowing readers to scan the live in-memory bitstream immediately without waiting for block finalization.

learningJourney.title: R · Representation: Delta-of-Delta Timestamp Encoding
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Shows how regular scrape intervals collapse 64-bit timestamps into 1 bit.

explanation.foundation: Suppose a Prometheus scraper polls a node every 60 seconds: `t0=0, t1=60, t2=120, t3=181`.
explanation.core: The first differences are `60, 60, 61`. The second differences (Delta-of-Delta `D`) are `D2 = 60 - 60 = 0` and `D3 = 61 - 60 = +1`. Gorilla uses a variable-length prefix code: `'0'` (1 bit) for `D == 0`; `'10'` + 7-bit signed `D` for `[-63, 64]`; `'110'` + 9-bit `D` for `[-255, 256]`; `'1110'` + 12-bit `D` for `[-2047, 2048]`; and `'1111'` + 32-bit `D` otherwise.
explanation.deepDive: In Facebook's production Gorilla deployment, ~96% of timestamps had `D == 0` (1 bit!), and nearly all remaining jitter fit inside the 7-bit bucket (`9 bits` total)—making timestamps practically free.

learningJourney.title: I · Invariant: IEEE-754 XOR Floating-Point Compression
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Explains why XORing consecutive floats beats integer delta encoding on floating-point values.

explanation.foundation: Subtracting two `float64` numbers (`42.3 - 42.1`) creates floating-point rounding noise across all 52 mantissa bits. Bitwise XOR (`v_{n-1} ^ v_n`) preserves exact lossless bit equality.
explanation.core: Gorilla computes `xor = prev_bits ^ curr_bits`. Case 1: `xor == 0` -> emit `'0'` (1 bit). Case 2: `xor != 0` -> emit `'1'`. If the non-zero meaningful bits fall inside the previous XOR's `[leading_zeros, trailing_zeros]` window, emit `'0'` + just those meaningful bits! Otherwise emit `'1'` + 5 bits (leading zeros, capped at 31) + 6 bits (meaningful bit count - 1) + the meaningful bits.
explanation.deepDive: Because monotonic counters and smooth gauges rarely change exponent or top mantissa bits, the XOR block shrinks to ~10–18 bits on average—and remains 100% bit-exact lossless upon `prev_bits ^ xor`!

codeExample.title: Gorilla Delta-of-Delta + XOR Value Encoder (Conceptual)
codeExample.code:
import struct

def float_to_u64(val: float) -> int:
    return struct.unpack('>Q', struct.pack('>d', val))[0]

def encode_xor_step(prev_u64, curr_val, prev_lead, prev_trail, bitwriter):
    curr_u64 = float_to_u64(curr_val)
    xor = prev_u64 ^ curr_u64
    if xor == 0:
        bitwriter.write_bits(0, 1)
        return curr_u64, prev_lead, prev_trail
    bitwriter.write_bits(1, 1)
    lead = min(31, (64 - xor.bit_length()))
    trail = (xor & -xor).bit_length() - 1
    if lead >= prev_lead and trail >= prev_trail:
        bitwriter.write_bits(0, 1)  # reuse previous window
        meaningful_len = 64 - prev_lead - prev_trail
        bitwriter.write_bits(xor >> prev_trail, meaningful_len)
        return curr_u64, prev_lead, prev_trail
    meaningful_len = 64 - lead - trail
    bitwriter.write_bits(1, 1)
    bitwriter.write_bits(lead, 5)
    bitwriter.write_bits(meaningful_len - 1, 6)
    bitwriter.write_bits(xor >> trail, meaningful_len)
    return curr_u64, lead, trail

learningJourney.title: M · Mechanics at Scale: 2-Hour Blocks & Random-Access Limits
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Explains why Gorilla chunks reset every 2 hours instead of compressing forever.

explanation.foundation: Gorilla encoding is stateful and sequential: to decode point #500, you must decode points #1 through #499 from the start of the chunk.
explanation.core: Resetting chunks every 2 hours (e.g., 120 points at 60s scrape, or 720 points at 10s scrape) bounds decode latency to microseconds and caps blast radius if a chunk is evicted or corrupted. It also aligns cleanly with Prometheus/VictoriaMetrics block compaction.
explanation.deepDive: Notice the 5-bit `leading_zeros` field only encodes values `0..31`! If a `float64` XOR happens to have 40 leading zeros, Gorilla clamps `lead = 31` so it never overflows the 5-bit field—trading 9 extra bits for a simpler fixed-width header.

decisionFramework.problem: How to store billions of streaming metric points in RAM with ~10x compression and sub-millisecond reads.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Store raw 16-byte structs or run Zstd on every incoming point.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Raw structs blow up DRAM by 11x; Zstd requires batching or burns CPU re-compressing tiny per-series buffers.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Raw arrays vs. Zstd batches vs. Gorilla Delta-of-Delta + XOR 2-hour chunks.
decisionFramework.decision: Use Gorilla streaming bit-compression per 2-hour chunk in RAM, then optionally apply Zstd/Parquet when flushing cold blocks to S3.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Sequential decode within a 2-hour chunk (mitigated by capping chunk duration at 2h) in exchange for O(1) append and ~1.37 B/point.

sectionDiagram.title: Open Chunk (Append Bits) -> 2h Seal -> Flush to Block Store

learningJourney.title: E · Edge Cases, Assumptions & When NOT to Use Gorilla
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Identifies out-of-order ingestion, noisy high-entropy floats, and NaN/Inf traps.

explanation.foundation: Gorilla assumes timestamps per series arrive mostly in order at regular intervals and values change smoothly.
explanation.core: When NOT to use Gorilla: (1) High-entropy random floats or cryptographic hashes—XOR windows stay near 64 bits wide, making Gorilla *larger* than 16 bytes due to control bits! (2) Heavy out-of-order writes—an append-only bitstream cannot insert `t_n < t_{n-1}` mid-chunk without rewriting or using an out-of-order buffer.
explanation.deepDive: Assumptions & Limitations: The ~1.37 bytes/point benchmark from Pelkonen et al. (VLDB 2015) assumes 60s scrape intervals (~96% `D=0`) and production monitoring gauges/counters where ~50%+ of consecutive values are identical or closely correlated. Glossary: Delta-of-Delta (second difference of timestamps), IEEE-754 (standard 64-bit float representation), Chunk (time-bounded compressed array for one series).

decisionExercise.prompt: A team uses Gorilla XOR compression on a time series of uniformly random 64-bit UUID hashes cast to floats. Compression ratio drops to 0.96x (worse than uncompressed!). Why?

options.label: Random values have zero bit correlation between consecutive samples, so XOR produces ~64 meaningful bits plus 13 control bits per point.
options.explanation: Correct! Gorilla XOR relies on consecutive float64 values sharing upper bits; uncorrelated random bits expand slightly due to header bits.

options.label: Gorilla only supports 32-bit integers.
options.explanation: Gorilla is specifically designed for 64-bit IEEE-754 floats.

options.label: 2-hour chunks are too short for XOR.
options.explanation: Chunk duration does not fix uncorrelated random entropy.

steps.explanation: Gauge value unchanged; entire (timestamp, value) point takes just 2 bits!

knowledgeChecks.question: In Gorilla timestamp compression, how many bits are needed to encode a timestamp whose Delta-of-Delta `D` equals `0`?

options.feedback: Correct! When scrape intervals stay constant (D=0), Gorilla emits a single '0' bit.
Gorilla operates at bit granularity, not byte boundaries.
32 bits is only used as a fallback for huge Delta-of-Delta jumps > 2048.
64 bits is only stored once for the chunk's initial anchor timestamp.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Regular 10s or 60s monitoring scrapes produce D=0 ~96% of the time, collapsing 64-bit timestamps to 1 bit.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does Gorilla use bitwise XOR (`prev ^ curr`) rather than arithmetic subtraction (`curr - prev`) for `float64` values?

options.text: IEEE-754 subtraction introduces rounding noise across mantissa bits, whereas XOR is 100% lossless and leaves upper sign/exponent bits as zeros.
options.feedback: Correct! `prev ^ xor` recovers the exact 64-bit float bit-for-bit.
CPUs have FPU subtraction, but it is lossy for compression.
XOR is only used on values, not timestamps.

options.text: Subtraction only works on negative numbers.
options.feedback: Subtraction works on all floats, just not bit-exactly.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Bitwise XOR is self-inverse (`(a ^ b) ^ a == b`), ensuring exact lossless float64 reconstruction.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does Gorilla cap each compressed chunk at a fixed 2-hour window instead of appending indefinitely?

options.text: To bound sequential bitstream decoding time and enable clean time-range eviction/compaction.
options.feedback: Correct! Because decoding point K requires scanning from the start of the chunk, 2-hour windows keep reads fast.

options.text: Because XOR only works for 120 samples.
options.feedback: XOR works for any sample count; the 2h cap is for query/retention bounds.

options.text: To force every query to scan S3.
options.feedback: 2-hour chunks stay hot in RAM specifically to avoid disk/S3 scans.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: 2-hour chunks balance compression ratio (~1.37 B/pt) with fast sequential decode and clean block aging.

beginner.summary: Gorilla shrinks time-series metrics from 16 bytes per point to ~1.37 bytes by storing only timestamp changes (1 bit when steady) and XOR bit differences for floats.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When storing regular-interval metrics in memory, compress timestamps with Delta-of-Delta and float values with XOR so you save ~90% of RAM.
beginner.byteSummary: Instead of saving full 64-bit timestamps and floats every 60 seconds, Gorilla stores a single '0' bit when the interval stays constant and only the changed bits of each new float.

intermediate.summary: Gorilla pairs Delta-of-Delta variable-bit timestamps (1/9/11/16/36 bits) with IEEE-754 XOR bit-windowing inside 2-hour chunks for ~1.37 B/point.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When building an in-memory TSDB buffer, use Gorilla Delta-of-Delta + XOR per 2-hour chunk for O(1) streaming writes and ~11x lossless compression.
intermediate.byteSummary: Delta-of-Delta collapses regular scrapes to 1 bit, while XOR window reuse keeps slowly changing float64 values compact inside 2-hour chunks.

advanced.summary: Bit-level Gorilla streaming encoder with 5-bit clamped leading-zero XOR windows, 2-hour chunk sealing, and out-of-order/high-entropy fallback awareness.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When deploying Gorilla compression at scale, cap chunks at 2 hours to bound sequential decode and route high-entropy or out-of-order streams to dedicated buffers.
advanced.byteSummary: Clamping leading zeros to 5 bits (`0..31`) simplifies the XOR control header while achieving ~1.37 B/point on smooth gauges; out-of-order writes and random entropy require separate handling.
